parent.name: Petrov's Defense
parent.overview: Black answers 2.Nf3 by counter-attacking e4 rather than defending e5. After 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.d4 d5 6.Bd3 both sides have lost an e-pawn and the structure is symmetrical, with the e-file the main open line. Black's aim is to equalise by quick development and piece trades; White tries to turn a small lead in development or slightly freer play into pressure, often castling and using the e-file or a queenside castling and pawn storm. The 3.d4 Steinitz line (3...Nxe4 4.Bd3 d5 5.Nxe5 Nd7) and 3.Nc3 (Four Knights transposition) or 3.d3 sidelines give quieter or more varied structures. The main lines are widely played at the top and are known as drawish, though some lines hold real attacking chances for both sides.

parent.name: Slav Defense
parent.overview: Black supports d5 with ...c6 so that the centre is held by pawns while the light-squared bishop stays free to come out (usually to f5 or g4) before ...e6. The root is a crossroads: after 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Nc3 Black chooses the Pure Slav with ...dxc4 (active bishop, ...e5/...c5 breaks), the Semi-Slav with ...e6 (c6-d5-e6 triangle, theory-heavy and often sharp: Meran, Botvinnik, Anti-Meran), or the Chebanenko ...a6. White can also play the Exchange (cxd5 cxd5), a symmetrical structure with queenside minority attack ideas that has a drawish reputation, or quiet systems with 3.e3 or 3.Bf4. The Slav is played by many world champions (Botvinnik, Smyslov, Anand, Kramnik) and is regarded as sound; sources treat it as solid with room for counterplay rather than a forced-draw defence.

parent.name: Scotch Game
parent.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 exd4
parent.overview: White strikes at the centre on move three and, after 3...exd4 4.Nxd4, trades the d-pawn for Black's e-pawn, opening the position early and releasing the central tension (s2). White gets space and quick development, Black gets easy piece play and the choice between active set-ups: 4...Bc5 (Classical), 4...Nf6 (Schmidt) and, less often, 4...Qh4 (Steinitz). The structure is open from the outset, so the game turns on piece activity rather than pawn manoeuvring. It can be played either positionally or tactically depending on the line (s2, s3). Objectively roughly equal: the Classical and Schmidt lines give Black good chances of equality, while Mieses (5.Nxc6 bxc6 6.e5) and the Steinitz are sharper (s1). Kasparov revived it in the 1990s as a way of avoiding the heavy Ruy Lopez theory, and Carlsen, Kramnik and Aronian have used it since (s1, s2, s3).

parent.name: French Defense
parent.overview: Black plays ...e6 and ...d5, accepting a pawn chain and a space deficit in return for a sound position, and then hits White's pawn centre at its base with ...c5. The fight is over the dark squares d4 and e5. Black's problem piece is the light-squared bishop on c8, hemmed in by the e6 pawn; Black solves it by exchanging it or rerouting it (...b6 and ...Ba6, or ...Bd7 with ...Bb5/a4). White typically uses extra space for a kingside attack (f4-f5, and in the Advance the g4/h4 ideas) or expands on the queenside with a3-b4. Play is slower and manoeuvring, with a lot of pawn-break play. It has a reputation for solidity but a cramped early game for Black. The Winawer (3.Nc3 Bb4) is the sharpest branch, the Advance is the main fight in a locked centre, and the Tarrasch, Classical and Exchange are quieter. The root is one position after 1...e6 2.d4 d5; the structures differ strongly by branch.

parent.name: Caro-Kann Defense
parent.overview: Black plays ...c6 to support ...d5 and so challenges the e4 pawn with a sound pawn structure, while keeping the light-squared bishop free to come out to f5 or g4 before ...e6 (the French Defence's main drawback, at the cost of a tempo). Black accepts less space early and tends to get a resilient, hard-to-break structure with few weaknesses and good endgame prospects. Play is mostly positional and manoeuvring; it is called more solid and less dynamic than the Sicilian (s1). The Advance (3.e5 Bf5) and Panov-Botvinnik (3.exd5 cxd5 4.c4) lines are more combative, and the Advance became the most popular White try in the 21st century. Main branches: Classical (4...Bf5), Advance, Exchange, Panov, 4...Nf6 lines, Gurgenidze (...g6), Two Knights (2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3) and Fantasy (3.f3). This is a crossroads root after 1...c6; the pawn structures differ by branch.

parent.name: Nimzowitsch Defense
parent.overview: Black develops a knight on move one and invites White to build a centre, planning to undermine it with timely pieces and pawn breaks (...d5, ...e5 or ...e6). The most common reply to 2.d4 is 2...d5 with 3.exd5 Qxd5 (Scandinavian-type), 3.e5 Bf5 (French-Advance-like with a freed bishop) or the 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.d5 Ne5 line, which is French-like in structure. Alternatively Black plays 2...e5 (Kennedy Variation), which can transpose to the Scotch, or 2...e6/2...g6 (Franco-Hiva, Pirc connection) with flexible set-ups. Kasparov and Keene wrote it has never been fully accepted as dependable, but sources agree it is far from refuted; players choose it to escape preparation and play non-standard but often French/Scandinavian-like middlegames. Roughly 2% of games per Chessable.

parent.name: Sicilian Defense: Old Sicilian
parent.overview: 2...Nc6 develops the queen's knight, covers d4 and e5, and keeps both ...d5 and ...e5 available in one move. It is a crossroads: after 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Black picks the Sveshnikov (...Nf6, ...e5), the Accelerated Dragon (...g6) or a Taimanov/Classical set-up, all sharp and heavily theoretical with asymmetrical pawns. White can sidestep that with 3.Bb5 (Rossolimo, aiming for doubled c-pawns and positional pressure) or with quieter third moves. The positions filed under this exact root are only those quieter third moves (3.Bc4, 3.Nc3, 3.d3, 3.g3, 3.b3, 3.c3); the main 3.d4 and 3.Bb5 lines sit in separate named roots.

parent.name: Caro-Kann Defense: Exchange Variation
parent.overview: White exchanges on d5 and, after 3...cxd5, develops quietly (4.Bd3, 4.Nf3, 4.c3 or 4.Bf4) instead of fighting for a big centre. The structure is the Carlsbad structure of the QGD Exchange with colours reversed: White keeps a queenside pawn majority (a, b, c vs a, b), Black has the extra central e-pawn and the minority on the queenside, so the minority attack is Black's resource and White usually plays on the kingside with a knight outpost on e5 or the manoeuvre Nd3. Black develops the light-squared bishop to f5 or g4 before ...e6 and aims to trade pieces and equalise; White gets slightly better piece placement but less ambition than in the main lines. The Rubinstein line 4.Bd3 Nc6 5.c3 Nf6 6.Bf4 stops ...Bf5. Sources call it very positional, less ambitious than the main lines, a long-time Karpov favourite and difficult for Black to win against, and say it rewards understanding over memorisation.

parent.name: Pirc Defense
parent.moves: 1. e4 d6 2. d4 Nf6 3. Nc3 g6
parent.overview: Black plays 1...d6 and, after 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3, ...g6 and ...Bg7, letting White build the broad e4-d4 centre and then undermining it from the flanks with ...c5 or ...e5 (hypermodern: the bigger White's centre, the bigger the target). The root is a crossroads: 1...d6 can transpose to the Philidor (3...e5 or ...c6) or to the Modern. White's replies run from sharp (Austrian Attack 4.f4, 150 Attack 4.Be3 with Qd2, Bh6 and h4-h5, Byrne 4.Bg5, Bayonet h4) to unhurried (Classical 4.Nf3 with Be2 and castling, fianchetto). Typical play is imbalanced: White gets space and often a kingside attack, Black gets a solid fianchettoed king and counterplay on the queenside and with central breaks. It is sound but has a reputation for giving White chances; Kasparov doubted it for the top level (s1), though Caruana, Anand and Grischuk have used it (s2).

parent.name: Four Knights Game
parent.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Nc3 Nf6
parent.overview: Both sides develop both knights, so the root position is a symmetrical, classical tabiya from which White chooses the character of the game. The main branches are 4.Bb5 (the Spanish Four Knights), 4.d4 (the Scotch Four Knights), 4.g3 (the Glek System) and 4.Be2/4.Bc4 quieter alternatives. After 4.Bb5 Black can mirror with 4...Bb4 (the Double Spanish, highly symmetrical and drawish) or go for the Rubinstein 4...Nd4 for imbalance; 4.d4 exd4 5.Nxd4 Bb4 6.Nxc6 bxc6 7.Bd3 d5 leads to an open, more active game in which White usually keeps the initiative. The opening has a drawish reputation and often gives quiet positional play, although sharp variations (Belgrade Gambit, Halloween Gambit) exist. It was almost forgotten after the 1930s and enjoyed a renaissance in the 1990s; Short, Adams and Shirov have played it, and it is popular at club level because it needs little theory.

parent.name: Sicilian Defense: French Variation
parent.overview: 2...e6 is a gateway rather than a set-up: after 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Black chooses the Taimanov (...Nc6), the Kan (...a6) or the Scheveningen (...d6, ...Nf6), with 3.Nc3 giving the Paulsen/Kan/Taimanov move orders. Black opens the diagonal for the f8-bishop and prepares ...d5 or ...Nc6/...a6 in a flexible way, with a solid ...e6/...d6 pawn chain and queenside counterplay. The name 'French' is only a naming convention: the pawn structure is Sicilian, not a French one. White's main choice is 3.d4 (about 61% of moves at 2500); rarer third moves are 3.d3, 3.g3, 3.c3 and Westerinen's 3.b3 (Bb2, occasional in the 1970s). At higher levels play is heavily theoretical.

parent.name: Ruy Lopez
parent.overview: The Ruy Lopez is the most extensively developed Open Game. 3.Bb5 attacks the knight that defends e5, building indirect pressure on the e5 pawn without the Italian's vulnerability to ...d5. This root (3.Bb5) is a crossroads: after the most common 3...a6 (about two-thirds of games) the Closed Spanish (4.Ba4 Nf6 5.O-O Be7 6.Re1 b5 7.Bb3 d6 8.c3 O-O 9.h3) leads to a slow, locked-centre manoeuvring game; the Berlin (3...Nf6 4.O-O Nxe4) gives a solid, drawish endgame-flavoured structure; the Marshall Attack is a sharp Black pawn sacrifice. White's central plan is c3 and d4 plus the Nbd2-f1-g3 knight route, while Black counterattacks on the queenside (...b5, ...Na5, ...c5) or breaks with ...d5. Theory is the deepest of any 1.e4 opening.
